newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Smuggling checks slow HK-China oil trade.
newsitem.headline: Smuggling checks slow HK-China oil trade.

text.p: High stocks and a clamp on smuggling by Chinese authorities are slowing trade between Hong Kong and southern China's oil ports, industry sources said on Monday.

They said the two factors were causing shipping congestion and forcing prices lower as trade slowed. "Oil trade, especially diesel, has slowed significantly since the clamp down on smuggling," said a trader with a major oil firm in Hong Kong. "This, coupled with the limited Chinese oil imports, has caused trade to come to a near standstill."

Hong Kong officially exports about 200,000 tonnes of diesel to China each month. A lot of diesel purchased in the Hong Kong market is later smuggled into China. In April, Chinese authorities started a campaign to catch smugglers who try to avoid the $60 per tonne in taxes for diesel entering China. The drive was also part of an effort to tighten security ahead of Hong Kong's return to China on July 1.
Small 1,000- to 2,000-tonne lots of diesel for delivery to China from Hong Kong were priced around $206-$207 per tonne last week, down from $220 from a month ago, they said.

But China has also slowed imports because of rising stock levels at a time of increasing domestic output. China produced 15.4 million tonnes of diesel in the first four months of 1997, up 10.1 percent compared with a year-ago period, official Chinese figures showed. Imports in the first quarter were 793,252 tonnes, up 102 percent from the year earlier period. Traders estimated that before the clamp on smuggling, as much as half again was imported illegally.

The high stocks and increased policing of routes between Hong Kong and China has caused a build up in shipping traffic, hindering the movement of contractual deliveries between sellers and Chinese buyers.

"With more patrol ships plying the southern ports of China and more stringent checks, vessels delivering oil are delayed for a few days and this also deters genuine buyers," said an oil trader in Hong Kong.

"Traffic is likely to be heavier in Hong Kong in the next two weeks as more vessels arrive," he said. Traders said discharge delays could be up to five days. "About 11 ships are now queuing outside Fujian waiting to discharge," said a Singapore oil trader.
Just last week, two oil vessels of about 20,000 tonnes returned to Hong Kong because of high demurrage costs in China.
Traders were also concerned that the slow down in Chinese imports would undermine prices in the benchmark Singapore diesel market, eroding already pressured refinery margins.

Prompt lifting of Singapore gas oil fell on Friday below $25.00 per barrel -- the lowest level since last August, while crude prices have remained relatively stable. Traders said China was also under pressure to cut wholesale prices in the domestic market.
